interviewQuestions.question: What is training-serving skew, and how do feature stores prevent it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define it concretely: training-serving skew happens when the feature values a model learned from during training are computed by a different pipeline — often different code, a different language, a different team — than the feature values it receives at serving time in production, and those two pipelines disagree on some edge case even though they're meant to compute "the same" feature. A real example: training computes "days since last login" in a batch Python job with one timezone convention and null-handling rule, while serving computes it in a separate low-latency Java service with a subtly different rule — both look correct in isolation, but the model now sees systematically different inputs live than it learned from, degrading accuracy with zero errors thrown anywhere. Feature stores prevent this structurally: a feature is defined **once**, in one place, and both the offline store (used to build training datasets) and the online store (used for low-latency serving) are populated from that single shared definition — there's no second, independently-written implementation left to drift out of sync. They also add point-in-time correct joins for training data (so you don't accidentally leak future feature values into historical training rows) and feature versioning (so a live model keeps getting the exact feature version it was trained on, even as the definition evolves elsewhere).

**Testing:** whether you understand skew as a dual-implementation problem specifically, and can name the structural fix (shared definition) rather than a vague "consistency between training and serving" answer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Dual implementations as the root cause
